newsitem.title: GERMANY: BIS denies helping Nazis hoard looted gold.
newsitem.headline: BIS denies helping Nazis hoard looted gold.

text.p: The Swiss-based Bank for International Settlements (BIS) said late on Thursday it had not helped Nazi Germany hoard looted gold during the Second World War, nor was it on friendly terms with the German Reichsbank, or central bank, at the time.

In 1946 the BIS handed the Allied Powers 3.7 tonnes of gold which had been identified as plundered from the Dutch and Belgian central banks and had been paid to BIS by the Reichsbank, BIS general secretary Gunter Baer said.

"The BIS has been accused of being friendly with the German Reichsbank, that it didn't defend itself and made it possible for Germany to use it as a turntable for transactions," Baer told the Frankfurt International Economic Journalists' Club.
"These accusations are unfounded and based on what we know today there is no indication that this happened."

The BIS said in September it would cooperate with any competent authority -- such as a Berne-appointed commission of experts or Holocaust account panel -- that wished to examine its records with regards to the fate of Nazi gold.

The Basle-based BIS, central bank to the world's central banks, has been drawn into the current debate over the fate of Nazi gold because of its role in overseeing reparations from Germany to the Allied governments following World War One.
Baer said the Reichsbank had deposited 12 tonnes of gold worth $14-15 million in its account with the BIS between 1939 and 1945.
About half of the gold received was interest paid by the Reichsbank for BIS investments in Germany under the 1930 Hague Agreement and the Young Plan.
The remainder covered German debts in a European postal clearing system and payments to the Yugoslav railways, Baer said.
A further 1.5 tonnes of Reichsbank gold destined for the BIS had never physically arrived because Swiss authorities barred the shipment from Swiss territory, Baer said.
"If there was any more there must have been a secret gold book but I don't know of its existence and don't believe in it," Baer said.

Swiss bankers and politicians, embarrassed by allegations that their country profited from the Holocaust, are considering whether to create a fund for victims of Nazism as a gesture of reconciliation.

Financiers and politicians interviewed this week said debate was just starting in parliament and bankers were divided, but a fund was one option for responding to months of Jewish-led attacks on Switzerland's financial role in World War Two.
U.S. senator Alfonse D'Amato, chairman of the Senate banking committee, recently wrote to BIS general manager Andrew Crockett, asking the BIS to publish its records on Nazi gold.
In September the Swiss government endorsed an official inquiry into the whereabouts of both Nazi and Jewish wealth held by Swiss banks during World War Two.
